common_name: Taylor's Rudolph Yaupon Holly (Dwarf Mounding Red-Berried Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Taylor's Rudolph is a dense, dwarf, mounding female selection of native yaupon holly that fills out to the ground without the bare legginess of older seedling-grown plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; like other yaupon selections, Taylor's Rudolph tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and a wide range of soil types with ease, though it performs poorly in polluted urban settings. This fine-textured, dwarf cultivar forms a dense, naturally mounded shrub 3-4 feet tall and wide, filling out to the ground without the bare, leggy look that plagues many seedling-grown yaupons. As a female selection it sets a heavy crop of glossy red berries each fall that persist into winter, but it needs a nearby male yaupon cultivar such as 'Schillings' or 'Will Fleming' (or an unselected male plant) within pollinating range to fruit well. Its compact habit and light winter pruning needs make it a good choice for a foundation planting, low hedge, or mass planting where the straight species would quickly outgrow the space.

common_name: Hoskins Shadow Yaupon Holly (Cold-Hardy Large-Leaf Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Hoskins Shadow is a female selection of native yaupon holly notable for larger, darker leaves than typical yaupon and unusually good cold tolerance for the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the best berry set in full sun; Hoskins Shadow was selected at a Tennessee nursery for its unusually large, dark green leaves and for cold hardiness beyond what is typical of yaupon holly, reportedly tolerating brief temperatures well below the species' usual limits. It grows quickly into a dense large shrub or small multi-trunked tree, and as a female selection it produces heavy crops of scarlet-red berries that hold from fall through spring when a male yaupon is planted nearby for pollination. Like other yaupon selections it tolerates drought, salt spray, brief flooding, and a wide range of soils once established, and takes well to shearing if a more restrained size is wanted. Its combination of bold foliage and superior cold tolerance makes it a useful choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of yaupon's range.

common_name: Nigra Inkberry Holly (Large Dark-Leaved Native Broadleaf Evergreen)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Nigra is a larger, older inkberry selection valued for its especially dark, lustrous foliage that takes on a purplish cast in winter.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Nigra does not tolerate dry spells as well as some newer dwarf inkberry cultivars and benefits from mulching to keep the root zone evenly moist. This older selection grows considerably larger than compact cultivars like 'Compacta' or 'Shamrock,' reaching 6-10 feet tall and wide, with particularly dark, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves that take on a purple-black cast in cold weather. It shears well into a tall hedge or informal screen and is notably resistant to verticillium wilt and tolerant of salt spray, making it useful in seaside plantings. Only female plants set the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator such as 'Nordic' nearby for fruit production.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Ivory Queen Inkberry Holly (White-Berried Native Broadleaf Evergreen)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Ivory Queen is a naturally occurring white-fruited form of native inkberry, selected for its off-white to ivory berries in place of the species' typical black fruit.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Ivory Queen is a selection of the rare white-fruited natural form of inkberry (Ilex glabra forma leucocarpa), grown for its unusual off-white to pale ivory, sometimes pink-blushed berries rather than the glossy black fruit typical of the species. The densely branched, upright, arching shrub carries the same lustrous dark green, spineless leaves as other inkberry selections, providing a fine-textured, boxwood-like presence for a foundation planting or informal hedge. Like all inkberry hollies it is dioecious, and only female plants like Ivory Queen bear fruit, requiring a male cultivar such as 'Nordic' planted within range for pollination and a good berry display. Give it evenly moist, acidic soil, since inkberry performs poorly if allowed to dry out for extended periods.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Gem Box Inkberry Holly (Dwarf Globe Boxwood-Alternative Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gem Box is a dwarf, globe-shaped Proven Winners introduction bred to stay dense and full to the ground without the bare lower legginess older inkberry selections can develop.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, where it shows good shade tolerance despite performing best with several hours of direct sun. Gem Box forms a naturally tidy, dense, rounded globe of small, dainty, dark green leaves tipped reddish in the spring flush, staying leafy all the way to the ground and needing little to no shearing to hold its shape, which makes it a genuine native alternative to dwarf boxwood in a foundation planting, low hedge, or container. It is a female cultivar and will set the small black berries typical of inkberry if a male pollinator such as 'Squeeze Box' is planted within about 50 feet, though it is grown primarily for its compact evergreen form rather than fruit. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic, and apply an acid-forming, evergreen-type fertilizer in spring for best color and density.

common_name: Strongbox Inkberry Holly (Compact Mounded Boxwood-Alternative Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Strongbox is a compact, broadly rounded Proven Winners inkberry selection with shallow roots that benefit from a steady 2-3 inch mulch layer.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and avoid letting it dry out since it carries a naturally shallow root system best protected with a steady layer of mulch. Strongbox forms a dense, broadly rounded, flat-topped mound of leathery, deer-resistant dark green leaves that stays leafy to the ground, giving it a slightly wider, more squat silhouette than the globe-shaped 'Gem Box' selection it is often paired with. It is a female cultivar that produces small white spring flowers valued by pollinators, followed by black berries in fall and winter if a male pollinator such as 'Squeeze Box' is planted within about 50 feet. A low-maintenance, disease- and pest-resistant native alternative to dwarf boxwood, it needs only an occasional light prune after new spring growth to keep its neat, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Fortuniana is an old, large-flowered gardenia cultivar valued as one of the most free-blooming selections available, flowering over an unusually long season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, since too much direct sun can scorch the foliage and cause bud drop. Fortuniana is a large, vigorous heirloom gardenia cultivar bearing fully double, pure white flowers resembling small camellias, up to 4 inches across, with the same intense, sweet, classic gardenia fragrance shared by the whole genus. It is among the most free-flowering of the old gardenia cultivars, blooming heavily from mid-spring into summer and often sporadically beyond, on a large, dense, glossy-leaved shrub that can be grown as an informal hedge or specimen where it has room to reach 5-8 feet tall and wide. As with all Gardenia jasminoides, strongly acidic soil and consistent moisture are essential; iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves with green veins) signals insufficient soil acidity and is corrected with sulfur amendments and acid-forming fertilizer.

common_name: Professor Pucci Gardenia (Compact Long-Blooming Double-Flowered Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Professor Pucci is a compact, bushy gardenia cultivar noted for an unusually long bloom season, flowering from late spring through fall rather than a single spring flush.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in a sheltered site in full sun to partial shade, since young plants and open flower buds are sensitive to frost and strong wind at the cooler edge of the range. Professor Pucci is a compact, bushy gardenia cultivar prized for its unusually long flowering season, producing a steady succession of large, fragrant, creamy-white double flowers from late spring all the way through fall rather than the single concentrated spring flush typical of many older gardenia cultivars. Its dense, rounded habit and glossy evergreen foliage make it well suited to foundation plantings, mixed borders, or large containers where its extended bloom and classic gardenia fragrance can be enjoyed for months. Keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and apply an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season, since gardenias quickly show interveinal yellowing if the soil pH climbs too high.

common_name: Golden Magic Gardenia (Flowers Aging from White to Golden Yellow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Magic is a novelty gardenia cultivar whose double white flowers gradually age to creamy and then golden yellow as they mature, creating multiple flower colors on the shrub at once.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, since intense direct sun can scorch the glossy foliage and cause buds to drop. Golden Magic is a novelty gardenia selection grown for its unusual color-changing flowers, which open a fragrant, pure white and gradually deepen through creamy yellow to a rich golden yellow as they age, giving the shrub a two-toned display of white and gold blooms at once during the growing season. The compact, rounded, heat-tolerant habit fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, or large containers, and its intense classic gardenia fragrance carries as well as any other cultivar despite the unusual color break. As with all gardenias, keep the soil consistently moist and strongly acidic, watching for interveinal yellowing that signals iron chlorosis in insufficiently acidic soil.
